title: the DSG improving-play tail

banner.title: The DSG IMPROVING-PLAY TAIL: FIGHTING, DIVERSIONS, SPEEDING PLAY, SPELL USE, LANGUAGES, MAPPING, R529: printed pp. 60-63 (pdf 61-64) - the fighting effectively: characters fight better together long (experience and trust, but cooperative techniques practicable from the start), the well-organized party defining roles (the low-AC fighters between the monsters and the rest), the retreat plans (the rear guard, the pursuit-discouraging magic-user spell, the safe-path scout), the mini-teams (the fighter bodyguarding the mage who casts for the group; the diversion fighter drawing attention while the thief sneaks behind), and surprise probably the single most important tactic (scouting to avoid it, silent no-light movement to cause it; rangers least susceptible and most likely to cause it, human rangers grievously disadvantaged underground by their lack of infravision, half-elven rangers very effective); the creating diversions: a distraction can substitute for concealment (fires demanding immediate attention, collapsing bridges/tunnels/dams, the rope-topped statue), monsters not automatically falling for it - the low-Intelligence reasoning monsters like orcs and ogres distracted 1d4 rounds, the medium-to-high Intelligence allowed a saving throw vs. spell, the genius-level fooled only by very clever diversions concealing the PCs' presence, and player characters never saving against monster diversions (purely role playing); the speeding play: pace as group taste but wasted time a bane to all (squabbling, non-cooperation, DM-arguing, indecision), fixed by standard procedures - the door-opening drill (a sketch with each character's role, declared as "door opening drill #2"), the standard marching orders (corridor widths, open areas, weapons carried, changes communicated), the caller re-examined for frustrated groups (delegating to one member, rotating every session), and the bossy player best handled by peer pressure; the creative underground spell use: the balanced selection across offensive, defensive, restorative, investigatigative and scouting spells with reverses considered, the sleep protections (magic mouth, glyphs of warding, fire traps, rope tricks), the underground-deadly cloudkill/stinking cloud/dig/transmute rock to mud/disintegrate with augury/divination/find the path useful, the raise-water flood from high terrain and lower water against enemy boaters, the enlarge/reduce/warp wood passage tricks, the silence coin carried for the party and thrown among enemy spellcasters, the darkness against infravision creatures (dramatic with blindfighting proficiency), the telekinesis-positioned slime pots dropped as missiles or left in the path and broken with shatter, the charm-aided questioning of captives, and the toppling walls of stone/ice/iron with the ricocheting lightning bolt; the languages of the underdark: the UA undercommon and sign language plus the tapping language of the subterranean races (clicking stones, drum beats, sharp-sound patterns), the underground reverberations amplifying drum communication over very long distances, the roughly 10-times-slower pace, and the underground-native PCs knowing it; and the mapping techniques: the detailed 10-foot-block graphing standard (accurate but slow in game and real time, the mapper's light source exposing the party, the 10-to-20-foot map errors agonized over against teleport-trap worries), the exit-purpose rule making elaborate maps overkill, and the line-drawing alternative (lines for corridors, door symbols, guesswork distances, the explored-versus-unexplored display, the 100-foot sketch with temporary light, sufficient everywhere except mazes and convoluted cavern networks)
banner.provenance: the DSG scan (archive.org item advanced-dungeons-dragons-1st-edition), pdf = printed + 1; the text read from the IA djvu OCR (djvu.txt lines ~7848-8160) with the pdf Acrobat-Capture layer as the second read (idx 139-143 = the printed pp. 60-63 windows); the compiled-tables appendix has no reprint of this prose. A CLEAN-READ ROUND: both machine reads agree on every load-bearing number - the 1d4-round diversion distraction, the 10x tapping-language slowness, the 10-ft graphing blocks, the 10-or-20-ft map error, and the 100-ft sketch window. The only garbles are the standing glyph classes (the UA-lead djvu noise, the "5096"-class absent here). SEAMS: the Unearthed Arcana undercommon and sign language (cross-book), the blindfighting proficiency (R506), the ranger infravision (PHB class), the R518 water travel, and the R511 surprise rules. WITH THIS ROUND THE IMPROVING-PLAY CHAPTER CLOSES (all children 142-150 flipped, the parent 141 closeable at the next census check) - and the player half of the book through printed p. 63 is fully pinned. The DM's section (pp. 64-120, re-grained at R503) starts the NEXT round. Nothing auto-credits.
banner.sentinel: A prose round: no tables pin. The numbers pin as consts per the R508 convention: the 1d4-round diversion distraction, the 10x tapping-language multiplier, and the mapping numbers (the 10-ft blocks, the 10/20-ft error pair, the 100-ft sketch). The rest pins as prose bools: the fighting rules (the togetherness, the low-AC placement, the retreat plans, the mini-teams, the surprise paramountcy with the ranger note), the diversion tiers (the fire/sabotage/remote-control set, the low-Int 1d4, the mid/high save, the genius standard, the PC no-save), the speeding-play procedures (the drills, the marching orders, the caller rotation, the peer pressure), the creative spell tactics (the balanced selection, the sleep protections, the deadly set, the water spells, the passage tricks, the silence coin, the darkness, the slime pots, the charm, the toppling walls), the tapping language (the drum amplification, the native-PC knowledge), and the mapping styles (the graphing weaknesses, the exit purpose, the line-drawing alternative and its limits). The UA/R506/R511/R518 seams are noted; nothing auto-credits.

consts.name: dnpmDivertDice
consts.comment: the low-Intelligence distraction roll is one die.

consts.name: dnpmDivertSides
consts.comment: monsters with reasoning ability but generally low Intelligence, such as orcs and ogres, direct their attention toward a diversion for 1d4 rounds unless something else attracts them.

consts.name: dnpmTapLangMult
consts.comment: communication in the tapping language takes approximately 10 times as long as with any spoken language.

consts.name: dnpmMapBlockFt
consts.comment: the common mapping style is the detailed graphing of each 10-foot block of corridor explored or room entered.

consts.name: dnpmMapErrLowFt
consts.comment: when a room overlaps a mapped corridor, the most likely explanation is that the map is off by 10 or 20 feet - not teleport traps.

consts.name: dnpmMapErrHighFt
consts.comment: the upper end of the likely 10-to-20-foot map error.

consts.name: dnpmSketchFt
consts.comment: with a line-drawing map the light is shone temporarily while the mapper quickly sketches in the last 100 feet of corridor, then extinguished while the party advances.

bools.name: dnpmFightTogetherLonger
bools.comment: characters fight more effectively if they have been together for a long time - a natural outgrowth of experience revealing strengths and weaknesses, and trust as companions learn to rely on each other; but cooperative techniques can be practiced from the very start.

bools.name: dnpmLowAcInFront
bools.comment: a well-organized party defines combat roles suited to strengths - at the most basic level, keeping the fighters with low Armor Class between the monsters and the rest of the party.

bools.name: dnpmRetreatPlans
bools.comment: sophisticated planning includes simple tactical plans: who takes the rear guard in a retreat, what magic-user spell confuses or discourages pursuit, who scouts the safe path of retreat.

bools.name: dnpmMiniTeams
bools.comment: characters benefit from mini-teams within the party: a fighter bodyguarding the magic-user who then casts for the group's benefit, or a fighter creating a diversion at combat's start while a thief waits to sneak behind the foe.

bools.name: dnpmSurpriseParamount
bools.comment: probably no single tactic is as important as surprise: effective scouting best avoids being surprised, and moving silently without light sources is the best way to surprise an opponent.

bools.name: dnpmRangerInfravisionNote
bools.comment: ranger characters are the least susceptible to surprise and the most likely to cause it - but human rangers underground suffer grievous disadvantages from their lack of infravision, while half-elven rangers are very effective in this environment.

bools.name: dnpmDiversionNoConceal
bools.comment: surprise depends on keeping presence secret, but a diversion created or taken advantage of can distract a foe so thoroughly that the PCs can approach with little regard for stealth - fires (needing immediate attention), sabotage like collapsing a bridge, tunnel, or dam, and remote-control tricks like the rope-tied statue yanked to topple.

bools.name: dnpmIntelligentMonstersWary
bools.comment: monsters - particularly intelligent ones - do not automatically fall for diversions.

bools.name: dnpmMidHighIntSave
bools.comment: monsters of medium to high Intelligence are allowed a saving throw vs. spell to see whether they are fooled by a diversion.

bools.name: dnpmGeniusNeedsClever
bools.comment: monsters of genius-level Intelligence can only be fooled by very clever diversions in which the PCs' presence is not easily discerned.

bools.name: dnpmPcNoSaveVsDiversion
bools.comment: player characters never get a saving throw if a monster uses a diversion against them - whether the PCs fall for it is purely a matter of role playing.

bools.name: dnpmPaceGroupTaste
bools.comment: the pace of a gaming session is a matter of group taste - rapid plot-advancers and savor-every-decision players alike - a healthy diversity and a strength of role-playing gaming.

bools.name: dnpmWastedTimeBane
bools.comment: wasted time is a bane to all campaigns: squabbling among players, failure to cooperate, incessant arguing with the DM, and failure to decide on a course of action.

bools.name: dnpmDoorDrills
bools.comment: the rate of play increases with standard procedures: door-opening drills adopted and standardized, with a rough sketch of each PC's location and each character's role (guarding the rear, picking the lock, ready to shoot) defined for the DM - then a simple declaration ("door opening drill #2") suffices.

bools.name: dnpmMarchingOrders
bools.comment: standard marching orders for common environments should be prepared and sketched: corridors of various widths, large open areas, and standard weapons carried while marching - changes simply communicated to the DM.

bools.name: dnpmCallerRotation
bools.comment: the caller idea (the character declaring the whole group's actions) should be re-examined if players are frustrated with the pace - experienced players delegate easily, the caller keeps the party moving through decision lulls, and the task works best rotating through the group every game session.

bools.name: dnpmBossyPeerPressure
bools.comment: if a player attempts to dominate play, peer pressure is probably the most effective method - the other players and the DM pointing out the effect of the bossy player's pronouncements.

bools.name: dnpmBalancedSpellSelection
bools.comment: all spellcasters should briefly discuss selections so the party winds up balanced across offensive, defensive, restorative, investigatigative, and scouting spells, considering the applications of reverses of reversible spells.

bools.name: dnpmSleepProtections
bools.comment: the protective benefits of magic mouth, glyphs of warding, fire traps, and rope tricks should not be overlooked when preparing to sleep.

bools.name: dnpmDeadlyUndergroundSpells
bools.comment: in an underground environment cloudkill, stinking cloud, dig, transmute rock to mud, and disintegrate can all prove deadly to an enemy - and augury, divination, and find the path are very useful underground.

bools.name: dnpmWaterSpells
bools.comment: from the high terrain a timely raise water spell can call down a sizable flood, and lower water can cause serious problems for enemy boaters.

bools.name: dnpmEnlargeReduceWarp
bools.comment: enlarge spells often effectively block a passageway, reduce can remove a barrier, and warp wood has a similar effect on doors.

bools.name: dnpmSilenceCoin
bools.comment: a silence spell cast upon a coin or small gem benefits the party when carried - and in an encounter the coin can be thrown among enemy spellcasters to silence their spell use.

bools.name: dnpmDarknessVsInfravision
bools.comment: darkness is effective when humans without a light source encounter creatures with infravision - and if characters are proficient in blindfighting, the darkness spell (which blinds infravision as well) can be quite dramatic.

bools.name: dnpmTelekinesisPots
bools.comment: green slimes and other deadly creatures sealed into clay or wax pots can be positioned with telekinesis over the enemy and dropped as missiles - or the pots left in the attacker's path and broken with shatter spells, or hurled without any spell.

bools.name: dnpmCharmQuestioning
bools.comment: the use of charm spells can immeasurably aid the questioning of captured monsters and other enemies.

bools.name: dnpmTopplingWallsRicochet
bools.comment: walls of stone, ice, and iron can be cast so they immediately topple and crush monsters within the area of effect, and ricocheting a lightning bolt can cause dramatic if somewhat unpredictable results.

bools.name: dnpmTappingLanguage
bools.comment: in addition to the Unearthed Arcana undercommon and sign language, the subterranean races have evolved a language based on patterns of tapping - expressed by clicking stones together, beating on a drum, or any pattern of sharp sounds.

bools.name: dnpmDrumAmplification
bools.comment: because underground passages create amplified reverberations, the tapping language enables communication over very long distances when drums are used - and player characters from the underground know this language.

bools.name: dnpmGraphingWeaknesses
bools.comment: the detailed 10-foot-block graphing style, while usually providing a reasonable copy of the DM's map, requires a great deal of game and real time (carefully paced dimensions, accurate recording), and forces a light source for the mapper that makes the party easier to spot.

bools.name: dnpmOverlapAgonizing
bools.comment: players tend to agonize over minor map errors - a room overlapping a mapped corridor provokes teleport-trap worries when the most likely explanation is a 10-or-20-foot map error.

bools.name: dnpmMapPurposeExit
bools.comment: the main purpose of the map is showing the characters the way out of the dungeon after the adventure - elaborate illustration is overkill unless careful attention to dimensions is necessary for some reason.

bools.name: dnpmLineDrawingMap
bools.comment: a line-drawing map works very well when exact dimensions do not matter: the mapper draws a line for the corridor path, standard symbols for doors, additional lines for branches, and educated guesswork for distances - serving admirably for retracing steps and displaying explored versus unexplored areas.

bools.name: dnpmLineMapLimits
bools.comment: a line-drawing map provides insufficient information in an extremely complicated or confusing area such as a maze or a convoluted network of caverns - other than these cases, every bit as effective and a lot more convenient than the graph paper masterpiece.
